Wheeled motor vehicle, usually four-wheeled, designed mainly to carry people on roads. Most definitions say a car seats 1–8 people and transports passengers rather than cargo; more than 1.6 billion were in use worldwide as of 2025.

The French inventor Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot built the first steam-powered road vehicle in 1769, a three-wheeled dray that hauled artillery at walking pace. In 1808 the Swiss inventor François Isaac de Rivaz built the first internal-combustion automobile. The modern car, a practical and marketable vehicle for everyday use, dates from 1886, when the German inventor [[Carl Benz]] patented his Benz Patent-Motorwagen; by the end of the 19th century he was selling 500 a year of later versions. The 1901 Oldsmobile Curved Dash and the 1908 [[Ford Model T]] are widely considered the first mass-produced and mass-affordable cars. Cars quickly replaced horse-drawn carriages in the U.S., while demand in Europe and elsewhere did not rise until after World War II. Use is still increasing rapidly, especially in China and India.

Most cars in the early 2020s are propelled by an [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engine]] burning [[Fossil fuel|fossil fuels]]. Electric cars, which competed with petrol and steam cars early in the 20th century, became commercially available again in the 2000s and widespread in the 2020s.

Cars bring personal mobility and independence and support large industries, but [[Traffic collision|traffic collisions]] are the largest cause of injury-related deaths worldwide. As of 2024, cars produce 10% of global [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] emissions, contributing to [[Climate change|climate change]]. Other costs include [[Air pollution|air pollution]], congestion, and urban sprawl.

Organic compound that is a sugar (saccharide), a polysaccharide such as starch, or a derivative of these, and one of the major families of biomolecules. For many carbohydrates, such as simple sugars, the carbon-to-hydrogen-to-oxygen atomic ratio is 1:2:1, giving the empirical formula CH₂O and molecular formulas of the form Cₙ(H₂O)ₙ. The other major families are [[Amino acid|amino acids]], fats, and [[Nucleic acid|nucleic acids]].

Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates and cannot be hydrolyzed to smaller ones. Disaccharides such as sucrose and polysaccharides or oligosaccharides such as starch and cellulose are classified by degree of polymerization.

Carbohydrates have numerous roles in living organisms. Polysaccharides store energy, as [[Starch|starch]] and [[Glycogen|glycogen]] do, and give structure, as [[Cellulose|cellulose]] does in plants and [[Chitin|chitin]] in arthropods and fungi. The 5-carbon sugar ribose is the backbone of [[RNA]] and a component of the coenzymes ATP, FAD, and NAD.

In nutrition, starch is abundant in cereals, potatoes, and foods made from flour. Sugars in the human diet are mainly table sugar ([[Sucrose|sucrose]], extracted from sugarcane or sugar beets), lactose in milk, and glucose and fructose, which occur in honey and many fruits.

Sugar cane was first grown in New Guinea and was mass-cultivated in India, reaching Europe around the 13th century. Constantin Kirchhoff discovered in 1811 that grape sugar (glucose) forms when starch is boiled with acid. The German chemist Carl Schmidt proposed the term "carbohydrate" in 1844, and the French physiologist Claude Bernard discovered glycogen in 1856. Emil Fischer received the 1902 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on sugars.

Chemical compound of one carbon atom double-bonded to two oxygen atoms, formula CO₂; a colorless, odorless gas at room temperature. The molecule is linear and centrosymmetric. Solid carbon dioxide, dry ice, exists below −78.5 °C at atmospheric pressure.

It is a trace gas in Earth's atmosphere at 428 parts per million (ppm), about 0.043%, as of July 2025, up from pre-industrial levels of 280 ppm, about 0.028%. Burning of [[Fossil fuel|fossil fuels]] is the main cause of the increase, which is the primary cause of [[Climate change|climate change]]. Transparent to visible light, CO₂ absorbs [[Infrared|infrared]] radiation and so acts as a [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gas]]. About half of excess emissions are absorbed by land and ocean carbon sinks, which can saturate and are volatile.

As the source of carbon in the carbon cycle, atmospheric CO₂ is the primary carbon source for life. Plants, algae, and cyanobacteria use sunlight to make [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrates]] from CO₂ and water by [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], releasing oxygen; aerobic organisms release CO₂ by respiration, and it is also released by decay and combustion. It is soluble in water, where it reversibly forms carbonic acid, a weak acid, though most dissolved CO₂ remains as CO₂ molecules. Dissolved CO₂ forms [[Carbonate|carbonate]] and mainly bicarbonate, which causes ocean acidification as atmospheric levels rise.

Nearly all CO₂ produced by humans goes into the atmosphere. Less than 1% of annual production is put to commercial use, mostly in the fertilizer industry and in enhanced oil recovery. Other uses include food and beverage production, cooling, fire suppression, greenhouse plant growth, and inert atmospheres for [[Welding|welding]].

Nonmetallic chemical element, symbol C, atomic number 6, in group 14 of the [[Periodic table|periodic table]]. Its name comes from Latin *carbo* 'coal'. It is tetravalent, its atoms able to form up to four covalent bonds through four valence electrons, and it has been known since antiquity.

Carbon makes up about 0.025 percent of Earth's crust and is the 15th most abundant element there. It is the fourth most abundant element in the universe by mass, after hydrogen, helium, and oxygen, and the second most abundant in the human body by mass (about 18.5%) after oxygen. Three [[Isotope|isotopes]] occur naturally: ¹²C and ¹³C are stable, while ¹⁴C is a radionuclide with a half-life of 5,700 years, used in [[Radiocarbon dating|radiocarbon dating]]. Its abundance, the diversity of its organic compounds, and its unusual ability to form polymers at Earth temperatures make it the common element of all known life.

Carbon bonds together in many ways, producing allotropes that include [[Graphite|graphite]], [[Diamond|diamond]], amorphous carbon, and fullerenes. Their properties differ widely. Graphite is opaque, black, soft enough to streak paper, and a good electrical conductor. Diamond is highly transparent, the hardest naturally occurring material known, and a poor electrical conductor. Diamond, [[Carbon nanotube|carbon nanotubes]], and [[Graphene|graphene]] have the highest thermal conductivities of all known materials. All allotropes are solid under normal conditions and chemically resistant. Carbon has no melting point at atmospheric pressure, since its triple point lies at 10.8 ± 0.2 megapascals and 4,600 ± 300 K; it sublimes at about 3,900 K (3,630 °C).

The most common oxidation state in inorganic compounds is +4, and +2 occurs in carbon monoxide. Carbon forms over a hundred million described compounds and is the basis of [[Organic chemistry|organic chemistry]].

Game in which cards are the primary device of play, whether the cards are of a traditional design or created specifically for the game. Countless card games exist, including families of related games such as poker.

Traditional games use a deck or pack of cards identical in size and shape, with indistinguishable backs. Because each card is identifiable from one side only, players know only their own cards, so card games are often characterized as games of "imperfect information." In board games, by contrast, cards serve a secondary purpose. Families of games include trick-taking games, shedding games, melding games such as rummy, vying games such as [[Poker|poker]], patience or solitaire games, and banking games such as [[Blackjack|blackjack]].

Playing cards were likely invented in China during the [[Tang dynasty|Tang dynasty]] around the 9th century. The scholar [[Ouyang Xiu]] associated a Tang "leaf game" with printed sheets, though he also claimed the "leaves" were pages used in a dice board game. The earliest dated instance of a game involving cards is 17 July 1294, when officials of the [[Yuan dynasty|Yuan dynasty]] caught two gamblers playing with paper cards.

The earliest European mention is in 1371, in a Catalan rhyme dictionary, perhaps reflecting maritime trade with the [[Mamluk]] rulers of Egypt. The first card game described in a document dates from 1408, and the earliest named game is Karnöffel, first mentioned in 1426. Two major innovations followed the arrival of trick-taking games in the late 14th century: trump cards and bidding. Trumps first appeared in [[Tarot]] packs. Collectible formats such as [[Magic: The Gathering]] emerged in the 1990s.

Any disease involving the heart or blood vessels; abbreviated CVD. It includes [[Coronary artery disease|coronary artery disease]], [[Heart failure|heart failure]], hypertensive heart disease, valvular heart disease (such as rheumatic heart disease), cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, congenital heart disease, aortic aneurysms, peripheral artery disease, and venous thrombosis.

Mechanisms vary by disease. Coronary artery disease, [[Stroke|stroke]], and peripheral artery disease involve [[Atherosclerosis|atherosclerosis]], which may be caused by [[Hypertension|high blood pressure]], smoking, [[Obesity|obesity]], high cholesterol, [[Diabetes|diabetes mellitus]], poor diet, lack of exercise, excessive alcohol consumption, and poor sleep. Estimates attribute about 13% of CVD deaths to high blood pressure, 9% to tobacco, 6% to diabetes, 6% to lack of exercise, and 5% to obesity; dietary risk factors are associated with 53%. Rheumatic heart disease may follow untreated strep throat.

Up to 90% of CVD may be preventable through healthy eating, exercise, avoiding tobacco smoke, limiting alcohol, and treating blood pressure, lipids, and diabetes. The use of [[Aspirin|aspirin]] in otherwise healthy people is of unclear benefit.

CVD is the leading cause of death worldwide except Africa. It caused 17.9 million deaths (32.1%) in 2015, up from 12.3 million (25.8%) in 1990. Death rates from CVD have fallen in most developed countries since the 1970s but are increasing in much of the developing world. Coronary artery disease and stroke account for 80% of CVD deaths in males and 75% in females. At the same age, men are about 50% more likely to develop CVD and are typically diagnosed seven to ten years earlier than women.

Geopolitical region in the middle of the Americas, centered on the [[Caribbean Sea]] in the North Atlantic Ocean of islands, cays, reefs, banks, and adjoining mainland coasts. It largely overlaps the West Indies, a term often used interchangeably.

Island arcs mark its northern and eastern edges: the [[Greater Antilles]] in the north and the [[Lesser Antilles]], including the Leeward and Windward Islands, to the east and south. The northwestern Lucayan Archipelago, made up of [[The Bahamas]] and the Turks and Caicos Islands, and [[Barbados]] are counted as Caribbean though they do not border the sea. Mainland coasts from the Yucatán Peninsula to the Guianas are included. The region is organized into 33 political entities, including 13 sovereign states, 12 dependencies, and 7 overseas territories. It is named for the Caribs, an Amerindian people of the Lesser Antilles.

The oldest evidence of humans is at Banwari Trace in southern Trinidad, where remains date from 7,000 years ago. Spanish explorer [[Christopher Columbus]] landed in 1492, beginning colonization by Spain, France, Britain, the Netherlands, and Denmark. Plantation economies grew sugar, tobacco, and coffee using enslaved Africans brought by the [[Atlantic slave trade]]. Revolution in [[Haiti]] against France in 1804 was the first successful slave revolt in the Americas. Most British, French, and Dutch colonies gained sovereignty between the 1960s and 1980s.

European colonization, the slave trade, indentured servitude, and later immigration have made the Caribbean one of the most ethnically diverse regions in the world.

German polymath active as a mathematician, astronomer, geodesist, and physicist. A child prodigy from a family of low social status in Brunswick, he studied with the Duke of Brunswick's support. From 1807 until his death he was director of the Göttingen Observatory and professor of astronomy.

His masterpieces were *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* and *Theoria motus corporum coelestium*. In number theory he contributed the composition law and the law of quadratic reciprocity, and he introduced the symbol ≡ for congruence. He gave the second and third complete proofs of the [[Fundamental theorem of algebra|fundamental theorem of algebra]]. At 19 he proved the construction of the regular heptadecagon, the first progress in regular polygon construction in over 2000 years. He introduced Gaussian curvature and proved the *Theorema Egregium*, and he introduced the normal, or Gaussian, distribution. He was the first to discover and study [[Non-Euclidean geometry|non-Euclidean geometry]], which he named, and he developed a [[Fast Fourier transform|fast Fourier transform]] some 160 years before Cooley and Tukey. More than 100 mathematical and scientific concepts bear his name.

He was instrumental in identifying [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]]. His work on the motion of planetoids led to the method of [[Least squares|least squares]], which he discovered before [[Adrien-Marie Legendre]] published it. He led the geodetic survey of the Kingdom of Hanover from 1820 to 1844 and made the first absolute measurement of Earth's magnetic field in 1832. His inventions included the heliotrope in 1821, a magnetometer in 1833, and, with Wilhelm Eduard Weber, the first electromagnetic telegraph in 1833.

He received the Lalande Prize in 1809 and the Copley Medal in 1838. He withheld incomplete work, delaying the spread of many discoveries. A reluctant teacher, he nonetheless taught [[Richard Dedekind]] and [[Bernhard Riemann]].

World's largest inland body of water, also described as the largest lake, in an [[Endorheic basin|endorheic basin]] between Europe and Asia. Its surface area is 371,000 km² (excluding the highly saline Garabogazköl lagoon) and its volume 78,200 km³. It stretches 1,200 km north to south with an average width of 320 km, and its surface lies about 27 m below sea level. Salinity is approximately 1.2% (12 g/L), about a third that of average seawater.

The sea is bounded by [[Kazakhstan]] to the northeast, [[Russia]] to the northwest, [[Azerbaijan]] to the southwest, [[Iran]] to the south, and [[Turkmenistan]] to the southeast. Its main freshwater inflow is the [[Volga]], Europe's longest river, which enters at the shallow north end. The name comes from the ancient Caspi people. Several states have called its status neither fully sea nor lake; a 2018 convention on its legal status set out cooperative management of resources.

The South Caspian Basin is a remnant of the ancient Paratethys Sea and has an oceanic basalt floor. The sea is estimated to be about 30 million years old and became landlocked in the Late Miocene, about 5.5 million years ago, through tectonic uplift and a fall in sea level.

The sea is home to a wide range of animal species, including [[Sturgeon|sturgeon]], and is famous for its caviar and oil industries. Pollution from the oil industry and dams on rivers draining into it have harmed its ecology. Its depth is predicted to decrease by 9–18 m during the 21st century because of global warming and desertification, a change described as leading to ecocide.

Small domesticated carnivorous mammal (*Felis catus*), also called the domestic cat or house cat, and the only domesticated species of the family [[Felidae]]. It belongs to the order [[Carnivora]]. An obligate carnivore, it has retractable claws adapted to killing small prey such as mice and rats, a strong flexible body, quick reflexes, sharp teeth, and well-developed night vision and sense of smell. It is a social species but a solitary, crepuscular hunter. It communicates by meowing, purring, trilling, hissing, growling, body language, and scent marking, and it secretes and perceives pheromones.

The name *Felis catus* was proposed by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1758. In 2017 the IUCN Cat Classification Taskforce regarded the domestic cat as a distinct species. The genus *Felis* diverged from other felids around 6 to 7 million years ago. The domestic cat and its closest wild ancestor both have 19 chromosome pairs and roughly 20,000 genes.

It was long thought that [[Domestication|domestication]] began in [[Ancient Egypt]], where cats were venerated from around 3100 BC. The earliest known indication of taming, however, is an African wildcat (*Felis lybica*) excavated near a Neolithic grave at Shillourokambos in southern [[Cyprus]], dating to about 7500–7200 BC. Scientists assume wildcats were drawn to early settlements in the [[Fertile Crescent]] by rodents, in particular the [[House mouse|house mouse]].

Today cats occur across the globe. Of an estimated 600 million domestic cats worldwide, 400 million live in Asia, including 58 million in China; about 73.8 million live in the United States. Feral cats avoid human contact, and their growing numbers, driven partly by pet abandonment, have contributed to the decline of bird, mammal, and reptile species.
